episodes.title: Killing of Canny Clark
episodes.lead: The killing of Canny Clark was the shooting of a Black man by Sheriff H. C. Griffin and a posse at daybreak on Tuesday, July 31, 1900, near Dade City, Florida. According to the only report, Clark drew a revolver on the sheriff and the posse shot him dead, and an inquest returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Cornelins Hyman
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Cornelins Hyman took place at Pearlington, Hancock County, Mississippi, on July 30–31, 1900, when armed white men chased and shot at a Black youth accused of attacking an elderly white woman with an ax. He was arrested unharmed the next morning and jailed at Bay St. Louis amid threats of lynching.

episodes.title: Attack on Black timber laborers at Donivan (Doniphan), Missouri
episodes.lead: The attack on Black timber laborers at Donivan (Doniphan), Missouri, took place in late July 1900, when white residents of a town that allowed no Black inhabitants tried to drive out a crew of Black workers brought in by a St. Louis timber company. Several of the workers were roughly handled and some whites and Blacks were injured before the sheriff placed an armed guard around the laborers. Papers outside Missouri reported it as a near "race war," and a Virginia editorial cited it as proof that racial conflict was not confined to the South.

episodes.title: Lynching of Elijah Clark
episodes.lead: The lynching of Elijah Clark took place on July 23, 1900, when a mob took Clark, a young Black man accused of assaulting a 13-year-old girl, from the Madison County jail in Huntsville, Alabama, and hanged him. The mob, put at 1,000 to 2,000 men, used dynamite and a smoking fire to overcome Sheriff Fulgham, who was carried out unconscious. White papers told the story as a contest between a determined mob and a sheriff who would not give up his prisoner.

episodes.title: New Orleans race riot (1900)
episodes.lead: The New Orleans race riot of July 1900 was a series of white mob attacks on Black residents of New Orleans, Louisiana, after a Black man, Robert Charles, killed two police officers on July 24. Over four days mobs killed several Black people and burned the Thomy Lafon school for Black children. Esther Fields, a washerwoman beaten in her doorway, was among the wounded named in wire casualty lists, and a grand jury later indicted alleged mob leaders.

episodes.title: Florence lynching threat (1900)
episodes.lead: The Florence lynching threat was a demand by citizens of Florence, South Carolina, in late July 1900 that two Black prisoners charged with rape be returned to them from the state penitentiary in Columbia, a demand that state officials and a Columbia church paper read as the prelude to a lynching. Governor McSweeney refused, and the principal accused died in the penitentiary of wounds two days later. McSweeney cited the case in his re-election campaign as a lynching he had prevented, and a wire item printed in Wisconsin said he had called out the militia against a mob at the Florence jail.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Atkins
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Atkins took place at Blythe station in Richmond County, Georgia, in late July 1900, when a mob met a sheriff bringing Atkins, a Black man charged with assault and robbery, to the county authorities. Atkins escaped unharmed when the sheriff and his lawyer put him aboard a passing train, and the Savannah Morning News reported the episode as a case of officers who "outwitted the mob."

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Jefferson
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Jefferson was the beating to death of a Black man at Hirsch's wood yard near Houston, Texas, in the summer of 1900, probably in July. Several men described as "negroes" were charged in the killing, and one of them gave a sworn statement describing it. The Houston Daily Post called it a lynching when it reported that a second man, Charles Harris, was held on a murder charge for his alleged part in it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Hillsman
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Hillsman was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Knoxville, Georgia, in late July 1900. Hillsman, accused of attempting to assault a planter's 14-year-old daughter, was seized from officers who had brought him back for a preliminary trial, and his body was riddled with bullets. A coroner's jury reported that it could not identify any member of the mob, and the story circulated mainly as a short wire item.

episodes.title: Richmond, Texas, train assault
episodes.lead: The Richmond, Texas, train assault was an attack in the summer of 1900 on Black passengers on a Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway train bound for Houston, allegedly by drunken white men including J. B. and William Wheat. It became known through damage suits by Black plaintiffs that together sought more than $95,000.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Charles and the New Orleans race riot
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Charles and the New Orleans race riot was a series of white mob attacks on Black residents of New Orleans in late July 1900, set off when Charles, a Black man, was accused of shooting three policemen, and ended by his death in a burning house on Friday, July 27. Wire reports counted twelve dead and twenty-eight wounded, mixing mob victims with the officers and citizens Charles was accused of shooting. A grand jury indicted both white mob members and Black people accused of aiding Charles, and Black weeklies treated the riot as a national question.

episodes.title: Assault on a Black man in the Smithfield Red Shirt riot
episodes.lead: The assault on a Black man in the Smithfield Red Shirt riot took place on July 31, 1900, at Smithfield, North Carolina, when an unnamed Black man in the crowd at a broken-up Populist speaking was "handled roughly" during a fight between Red Shirts and Populists. The incident was reported in a single sentence of a Raleigh dispatch to the New York Sun, which gave neither the man's name nor any injury. Other accounts of the Smithfield disorder, Democratic and Populist alike, did not mention him.

episodes.title: Killing of Thomas at Yorktown, Texas
episodes.lead: The killing of Thomas at Yorktown, Texas, was the fatal shooting of a Black man described as an escaped convict on the morning of July 31, 1900, by a man the Houston Daily Post identified as Deputy Sheriff Farris. A justice's inquest accepted the shooter's account that Thomas had come at him with a razor, and two Texas papers carried brief dispatches on the case.

episodes.title: Wilson registration beating
episodes.lead: The Wilson registration beating was an attack in late July 1900 in the town of Wilson, North Carolina, in which "Red Shirts" beat an elderly Black man and his son "nearly to death" at a voter registration place. No deaths were reported, and the incident is known from a single sentence in a New-York Tribune dispatch that offered it as an example of Red Shirt intimidation of Black voters.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Thomas and George Campbell
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Thomas and George Campbell took place at Fairmont, West Virginia, on the night of August 11-12, 1900, when a crowd of several hundred went to the Marion County jail to hang the two young Black men, who were accused of shooting two Baltimore & Ohio railroad men that afternoon. Officers had already removed the prisoners, and the crowd searched the jail and dispersed. The two were moved to the Ohio County jail at Wheeling, where they were still held awaiting trial in mid-September.

episodes.title: Lynching of Avery Mills
episodes.lead: The lynching of Avery Mills took place on August 28, 1900, near Forest City in Rutherford County, North Carolina, when armed men took Mills, a young Black tenant farmer, from two officers carrying him to jail and shot him to death. Mills had been arrested that morning, accused of killing his white landlord, Mills H. Flack, a former state legislator. Accounts presented the killing as the fulfillment of Flack's dying wish, and the wire brief added that a mob went looking for Mills's wife.

episodes.title: Lynching of Scott at Bayou Vidal
episodes.lead: The lynching of Scott at Bayou Vidal was the killing of a Black man at Bayou Vidal, Louisiana, on or about August 4, 1900, by people of the neighborhood who suspected him of murdering a farmer. After being repeatedly sunk in the bayou on a chain until he confessed, he was sewn into a weighted sack and thrown into the water. Northern papers carried it as a "New Style of Lynching" because of the method.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Benjamin Pugh
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Benjamin Pugh took place in Brooklyn, New York, on the afternoon of August 23, 1900, when a crowd that gathered at his arrest shouted "Lynch him!" as police led away Pugh, a Black man accused of shooting and killing a white waiter, John Tietjen. Police took Pugh to the station unharmed, and he was arraigned for first-degree murder and held for the grand jury. New York papers covered the case in detail, a Washington paper headed its dispatch "A Lynching Averted," and a Richmond editorial used it to argue that the North was facing "the negro question."

episodes.title: Seizure of Tom Bibb by a Lincoln County, Tennessee, mob
episodes.lead: The seizure of Tom Bibb was the capture of a Black man near Fort Deposit, Madison County, Alabama, on about August 13, 1900, by a mob of Lincoln County, Tennessee, citizens who accused him of assaulting Mrs. Alonzo Gillham and carried him across the state line. Jailed under his captors' promise that he would be hanged if proven guilty, he was saved by an alibi from State Senator Ed L. Pulley and returned to Huntsville two weeks later.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Cater
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Cater took place at Doe Run (also spelled Doerun), Georgia, in August 1900, when an armed mob of about fifty men forced its way into the town jail at night, took out Cater, a Black prisoner charged with attempted criminal assault on a white woman, and shot him to death. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days, repeating the claim that Cater had confessed and been identified by the woman.

episodes.title: Liberty County race riot (1900)
episodes.lead: The Liberty County race riot was a wave of attacks on Black residents near Liberty City, Georgia, in August 1900, in which a posse killed a Black man, Charles Small, and white men whipped the occupants of many Black homes after a white man, Robert C. Curtis, was shot dead on August 15. Reports of the Black dead ranged from one to five, and the governor called out militia before the sheriff reported order restored on August 18; wire services called it a "race war."

episodes.title: Killing of Boston Frederick
episodes.lead: The killing of Boston Frederick took place in Campbell County, Georgia, near Fairburn, where a posse of citizens led by a deputy sheriff shot dead Frederick, a Black escaped convict, in August 1900. By the posse's account, he aimed a shotgun at them when they came to arrest him, and Georgia and Alabama papers reported the killing as a fugitive resisting arrest.

episodes.title: Boston Spur ambush killing
episodes.lead: The Boston Spur ambush killing was the killing of an unnamed 16-year-old Black boy, shot from ambush at Boston Spur, in east Grant parish, Louisiana, on the afternoon of Wednesday, August 15, 1900. The Alexandria Town Talk and the Colfax Chronicle both condemned the killing, and the Chronicle presented it as part of a wave of threats and shootings aimed at driving Black sawmill workers out of the area.

episodes.title: Arrest of Branch Payne
episodes.lead: The arrest of Branch Payne was an exchange of gunfire in New Orleans on the night of August 16, 1900, between two deputy sheriffs and Payne, a Black man they had come to arrest, after which a crowd of "angry citizens" gathered and was dispersed by police. Payne submitted to arrest and was jailed under double guard, and no injuries were reported. A Chicago Tribune dispatch, reprinted across the country, presented the incident as "another outbreak against the negroes" narrowly averted in the neighborhood where Robert Charles had been killed weeks earlier.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bud Howard
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bud Howard was a crowd's pursuit of William ("Bud") Howard, a Black man, through downtown Akron, Ohio, on the night of Saturday, August 11, 1900, after he shot a white man, John Forbes, at the corner of Main and Market streets. According to a wire dispatch, hundreds of men chased Howard shouting "Lynch him!" but he outran them, and police later arrested him in East Akron. Charged with shooting with intent to wound, Howard was moved to the Cleveland jail eleven days later, when a mob seeking another Black prisoner, Louis Peck, besieged Akron's city prison.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bud Wilson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bud Wilson took place on August 22, 1900, when a mob of white men chased a St. Joseph, Missouri, police officer and his Black prisoner for about a mile through the Chicago Great Western Railroad yards. According to the only report found, the officer's protection kept Wilson from being lynched, and he was afterward held at the police station.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Burrell Bland
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Burrell Bland was a threat made in August 1900 against Bland, an elderly Black farmer living near Woodbury, New Jersey, by the family of a white woman he had married in Camden. According to a Camden wire dated August 15, the bride's parents and friends followed the couple and threatened to lynch Bland unless he gave her up. No report of what followed was found, and the marriage itself drew more attention than the threat, appearing as a curiosity in papers from Delaware to the Dakotas.

episodes.title: Killing of Carson Hardy
episodes.lead: The killing of Carson Hardy was the shooting death in August 1900 of a Black man, believed to be Carson Hardy, whose body was found near Shell Creek, Tennessee, on the E. T. & W. N. C. railroad. Hardy had been arrested on suspicion of burning a barn and, according to the Johnson City Comet, was shot to death while in an officer's charge. The Comet ran the item under the headline "Foul Play Suspected," noting thirty or more bullet holes in the body.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Gant
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Gant took place at the Grand Army of the Republic state reunion grounds in Lincoln, Nebraska, on the evening of Friday, August 17, 1900, when a white mob of several hundred tried to seize Gant, a Black man, from police. Gant was accused of striking a special officer, Mart Howe, over the head with a billiard cue. Police beat back the mob with clubs and took Gant to jail, and he was later bound over to the district court.

episodes.title: Coenties Slip mob threat against Charles Uppher
episodes.lead: The Coenties Slip mob threat against Charles Uppher took place on 27 August 1900 in lower Manhattan, when a white crowd called for the lynching of Uppher, a Black seamen's boarding-house keeper, after he shot a white man. Police took him to the station unharmed, and the Sun called it "another race riot."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charley Wilson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charley Wilson took place near Mhoon's Landing, Mississippi, on the night of August 29, 1900, when a band of men hunting an accused murderer put a noose around the neck of Wilson, a Black man from Greenville. The men released him when they noticed a scar on his face that the man they sought did not have. The dispatch circulated widely in the white press as a story of mistaken identity, and the Kansas City American Citizen reported it twice.

episodes.title: Cheneyville regulation of Black residents (1900)
episodes.lead: The Cheneyville regulation of Black residents was a set of rules imposed on the Black population of Cheneyville, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, by a white mass meeting in August 1900 and enforced by a committee that ordered idle Black men to leave and closed their gathering places. The meeting followed the killing of a young white man, Bennie Wall, by a Black man, Joe Milton, whose lynching the parish sheriff prevented. Within days the committee had dive keepers ordered away and a young Black man publicly whipped, and the wire reported that "quite an emigration" had begun.

episodes.title: Shooting of Coot Miles
episodes.lead: The shooting of Coot Miles took place on August 9, 1900, in Phoenix City (also spelled Phenix City), Alabama, when Policeman John Moon shot Miles, a Black man, as he ran from an attempted arrest. Miles was hit in the lung at a distance of about 175 yards and was described as probably mortally wounded, though he was still alive that night. A Columbus, Georgia, dispatch carried the story to Birmingham and Savannah papers, one of which called Miles a "negro desperado."

episodes.title: Killing of Daniel Lee
episodes.lead: The killing of Daniel Lee took place on the morning of August 11, 1900, when O. D. Traylor, a guard at the Virginia State farm, shot and killed Lee, a Black convict, with a Winchester rifle. Traylor said Lee had been trying to escape from a work detail, and the coroner decided that no inquest was needed. Richmond and Norfolk papers reported the shooting the next day, and the Richmond Planet noted it a week later.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dave Richardson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Dave Richardson was a reported plan by a party of white men to storm the county jail at Tallahassee, Florida, on a Saturday night in August 1900, probably August 11, and lynch Richardson, a Black prisoner accused of killing a white farmer named Harmon Gray. Governor Bloxham ordered a local militia company, the Governor's Guards, to protect the jail, and no attack was reported.

episodes.title: Mob attack on Dock Thomas
episodes.lead: The mob attack on Dock Thomas was an assault in Chicago, reported in August 1900, in which a crowd of nearly a hundred men and boys chased Thomas, a Black Pullman car porter, off a dock into the lake and stoned him in the water. Police arrived before he was seriously injured, and the only report found said the crowd would probably have stoned him to death without them.

episodes.title: Killing of Edward Moore
episodes.lead: The killing of Edward Moore took place on August 24, 1900, at Brown's tank on the Norfolk and Western Railway in southwestern Virginia, when George Fitzwater, a deputy United States marshal and Baldwin Detective Agency man, shot Moore, a Black bridge hand, through the head while arresting him. A coroner's jury found the shooting accidental and Fitzwater was released. Accounts differed on why Moore was arrested at all, and the Richmond Planet answered the official account with the words "One Negro less!"

episodes.title: Chipley turpentine camp shooting
episodes.lead: The Chipley turpentine camp shooting was a night attack in early August 1900 in which about a dozen masked men fired into the quarters of a turpentine camp near Chipley, Washington County, Florida, whose occupants were mostly Black. One man was killed outright and four were wounded, two of whom were reported to have died later; a coroner's jury blamed unknown parties, and two farmers were jailed on suspicion. A Pensacola dispatch presented the shooting as the climax of a campaign to drive Black people out of the area, a picture the Chipley newspaper rejected as slander.

episodes.title: Flomaton shooting of two Black railroad workers
episodes.lead: The Flomaton shooting of two Black railroad workers took place at Flomaton, Alabama, in August 1900, when two Black men were badly shot and taken to Montgomery for medical treatment. How they were wounded was never established in the coverage, which offered two competing reports, one describing a fight with tramps in a box car and the other a clash between white and Black men.

episodes.title: Bob Bridges threat against Black miners at Franklin and Newcastle
episodes.lead: The Bob Bridges threat against Black miners at Franklin and Newcastle was an episode reported by the Seattle Republican, a Black weekly, on 31 August 1900, in which the paper described Bob Bridges, permanent chairman of a Washington "union convention," as ready to lead the convention's delegates to kill the Black men working in the mines at Franklin and Newcastle. No violence is reported to have followed, and the item survives only as an editorial argument against Black support for Bridges.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Goode in Appomattox County
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Goode took place in Appomattox County, Virginia, in August 1900, when a young Black employee on a farm, charged with attempting to assault his employer's wife, was threatened with lynching both during his pursuit and after his trial. When a jury sentenced him to 18 years in the penitentiary rather than death, there were "many threats of lynching," and the court had the sheriff take him to Richmond at once.

episodes.title: Lynching of Irvin Love
episodes.lead: The lynching of Irvin Love was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Norfield, Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the night of Wednesday, August 22, 1900. Love, accused of robbing and burning a house and said to have confessed, was taken from custody while awaiting the sheriff and found hanged from a gum tree the next morning. A New Orleans wire story carried the killing to papers in New York and Washington, while the Brookhaven Leader described how the sheriff had been decoyed away.

episodes.title: Threat against Galveston barber T. H. Thomas
episodes.lead: The threat against Galveston barber T. H. Thomas was a death threat that, by his own account, white residents of Galveston, Texas, made to Thomas, a Black barber, in August 1900 before he left for the National Negro Business Men's League convention in Boston. Thomas told the convention that the callers had promised to kill him on his return if he went in the interest of Lillian Clayton Jewett's anti-lynching league. No violence against him was reported, but the published account caused severe criticism of him at home, and a later dispatch said he hesitated to return for fear of a noose.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Betts
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Betts took place at Corinth, Mississippi, early on the morning of August 13, 1900, when a mob of about fifty masked men took Betts, a Black farm laborer, from the county jail and hanged him to a telegraph pole. Betts had been jailed the day before, accused of assaulting a ten-year-old white girl. A brief wire report carried the killing to papers across the country, while the local weekly gave a long account that endorsed it.

episodes.title: New York West Side race attacks of August 26, 1900
episodes.lead: The New York West Side race attacks of August 26, 1900 were assaults by groups of white men on Black residents around Amsterdam Avenue and West Sixtieth to Sixty-fourth streets in Manhattan, beginning before daybreak with the beating of James Arnold, a 55-year-old Black man. They followed the shooting of a white messenger boy, John Brennan, by a Black man known as "Lamplighter," and the Associated Press reported them nationally as "incipient race riots." Arnold and Alexander Balentine were badly beaten and a gang smashed the windows of a Black tenement, but no one was arrested for either beating.

episodes.title: Killing of James Biddle
episodes.lead: The killing of James Biddle was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff Bunnell at Bunnell Station, in southern St. Johns County, Florida, on or about August 22, 1900. According to a St. Augustine wire report, the only account found, Biddle had attempted to kill a woman and fired on the deputy before being shot through the heart as he ran. The item circulated in white papers in Georgia, South Carolina and Mississippi and in the Black Richmond Planet.

episodes.title: Vincinnes Hotel kitchen fight
episodes.lead: The Vincinnes Hotel kitchen fight was a clash between white cooks and Black waiters in the kitchen of the "Vincinnes Hotel" in Chicago on a Sunday morning in early August 1900, apparently August 5, after the cooks tried to beat a waiter named James Meadows. Several people were cut or struck, the kitchen was wrecked, and police took fifteen hotel employees away in a patrol wagon. The Indianapolis Freeman, the only paper found to report it, called the fight a "race riot."

episodes.title: Killing of James Offutt
episodes.lead: The killing of James Offutt was the fatal shooting of James Offutt, a Black man serving as a special policeman at a baseball game, by Lee Cozart, deputy marshal of Earlington, Kentucky, on the evening of August 19, 1900. Cozart was prosecuted by the Commonwealth and, after an examining trial before County Judge John G. B. Hall at Madisonville, was discharged. The Earlington Bee covered the case at length because both men were well regarded locally, and it printed the judge's full opinion.

episodes.title: Pursuit of James Wilson (Chicago, 1900)
episodes.lead: The pursuit of James Wilson was an incident on the night of August 23, 1900, in Chicago, Illinois, in which a street crowd chased Wilson, a Black ventriloquist, after mistaking the rag doll he used in his act for a white child he had kidnapped. Wilson escaped unhurt on a street car, and newspapers reported the episode as "a narrow escape from lynching."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jasper Hays
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jasper Hays took place at Sandfly Station, near Savannah, Georgia, on the morning of August 5, 1900, when an armed crowd of street railway men hunting the killer of a motorman held Hays, a Black man first named as the shooter, at gunpoint. Some of the men wanted to punish him on the spot, but he convinced them that his brother Seaborn had fired the shots, and he was handed to a patrolman and jailed. His brother was later arrested by officers and convicted of murder, while the Black Savannah Tribune condemned the armed gathering as an unlawful mob.

episodes.title: Flogging and shooting of Jim Strickland
episodes.lead: The flogging and shooting of Jim Strickland was a mob attack on a Black man in Henry County, Georgia, reported in a dispatch from Griffin dated August 18, 1900. A crowd gave Strickland 150 lashes and shot him four times, accusing him of threatening talk against white people; he was not expected to die. The Associated Press story ran in papers from Georgia to Maine under headlines that ranged from "Flogged For Threatening Whites" to "Worse Than Savages."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Milton and the Cheneyville resolutions
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joe Milton took place at Cheneyville, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, on the night of August 10, 1900, when an armed white mob hunted down and captured Milton, a Black man accused of killing a young white man, Bennie Wall. The sheriff refused to allow a lynching, and Milton was jailed at Alexandria, where he died days later. The case drew national notice mainly because a mass meeting of white residents then ordered idle Black men to leave town.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Scales
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Joe Scales took place in Rockingham County, North Carolina, in late August and early September 1900, after Scales, a 15-year-old Black boy, was accused of criminally assaulting the six-year-old daughter of a local farmer, John H. Huskey. Captured by the girl's mother at revolver point on August 24 and jailed at Wentworth, he was moved to the Guilford County jail for safety after threats of lynching were made. Papers in North Carolina, Virginia and Washington carried the story, most of them dwelling on the mother's capture.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Dickson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Dickson took place in Longview, Texas, in August 1900, when local citizens planned to take Dickson, a Black man charged with attempted assault on a white girl, from jail and hang him. Sheriff Howard moved the prisoner out of town before the mob arrived, and Texas papers reported the episode as a lynching foiled by the sheriff.

episodes.title: Killing of John Lowery
episodes.lead: The killing of John Lowery was the fatal shooting of a Black miner, John Lowery (also spelled Lowry), by Policeman Harry Messer at Keystone, West Virginia, on the night of August 1, 1900. Messer, who according to the dispatches had been attacked by Lowery with a knife, was reportedly acquitted as acting in self-defence at Welch the next day. Papers across the country reported it because Black residents, said to be a majority of the town, threatened to lynch the officer, and headlines warned of a "race war" among the coal miners.

episodes.title: Killing of John Williams by Newport News police
episodes.lead: The killing of John Williams by Newport News police took place in Newport News, Virginia, in early August 1900, when Policeman R. B. Payne fired after Williams, a Black man known as "Coffee", as he fled custody after a raid on a craps game. Williams was found dead about an hour later, and Payne was charged with murder. A police court judge dismissed the charge on the ground that an officer may shoot an escaping prisoner, and Payne returned to duty.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jones at Pocahontas, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jones at Pocahontas, Mississippi, was a mob gathering reported on August 8, 1900, to lynch a Black man named Jones who had been arrested the day before on a charge of assaulting a white woman. Sheriff Harding and a posse of deputies set out from Jackson to stop it, and the coverage does not report what followed.

episodes.title: Locust Point attacks on non-union Black dockworkers
episodes.lead: The Locust Point attacks on non-union Black dockworkers were assaults by white crowds on Black men who had taken the places of striking dockworkers at Locust Point, Baltimore, on August 12 and 13, 1900. A crowd bricked a streetcar carrying the replacement workers one night and stoned a gang of fifteen leaving the docks the next, until one of the Black men fired five shots and wounded three white men. The wire story ran in papers across the country as evidence that the Baltimore strike had taken an 'ugly aspect.'

episodes.title: Killing of Joseph Williams
episodes.lead: The killing of Joseph Williams took place at Marshalltown, Iowa, on the evening of August 27, 1900, when a Black drayman was shot to death by one of a party of drinking tramps after a quarrel over two young white girls. Wire reports presented Williams as a man killed for defending the girls and said Black residents were talking of lynching the killers. Two tramps, John Gray and Pat Dunn, were indicted for murder.

episodes.title: Killing of Lee Moore
episodes.lead: The killing of Lee Moore was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two officers at Junction City, Arkansas, in August 1900, while they were arresting him on a warrant. A coroner's jury exonerated the officers, and the story circulated as a short item in Arkansas state-news columns and, briefly, in Texas.

episodes.title: New York City race riot of August 1900
episodes.lead: The New York City race riot of August 1900 was a night of attacks on Black people by white crowds on Manhattan's West Side on August 15-16, set off by the death of Policeman Robert J. Thorpe, who had been stabbed during an arrest. Dozens of Black men were beaten or clubbed and Lloyd Lee was shot by a policeman, but no deaths were reported. Papers compared it with the recent New Orleans riot, and the conduct of the police, accused of joining the attacks, dominated later coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of Louis Gibson
episodes.lead: The killing of Louis Gibson was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Augusta, Georgia, policeman W. M. Belding on the night of August 25, 1900, during an attempted arrest. A coroner's jury found the next day that the killing was justifiable homicide. Two Georgia papers carried brief Augusta dispatches that presented the officer's account and described Gibson as a "desperate negro character."

episodes.title: Akron riot of 1900
episodes.lead: The Akron riot of 1900 was a night of mob violence in Akron, Ohio, on August 22, 1900, when a crowd of thousands tried to seize and lynch Louis Peck, a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a six-year-old white girl. Peck had been moved to Cleveland, and the crowd fought the police, looted a hardware store, and burned and dynamited the city building. Two children were killed and about twenty people wounded, and Peck was sentenced to life two days later in a hearing that lasted minutes.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Luther Thompson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Luther Thompson occurred in late August 1900, when Thompson, a Black tenant farmer jailed at New Decatur, Alabama, on charges of horse stealing and attempted criminal assault on a white woman, was reported in danger of being lynched by the people of Cedar Grove in Morgan County. No attack on him is reported, and the coverage does not show what became of him. A Birmingham paper's special dispatch was condensed by the wire and reprinted in papers from New Jersey to North Dakota, and a Black weekly in Kansas City predicted his death.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Mary Coleman
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Mary Coleman took place at Helena, Arkansas, in August 1900, when a policeman trying to arrest Coleman, a Black woman, shot her three times in the abdomen. She was reported "mortally wounded," and the brief account, which gave only the officer's version, ran in at least six Arkansas weeklies.

episodes.title: Meridian race riot (August 1900)
episodes.lead: The Meridian race riot was a disturbance at Meridian, Mississippi, reported in August 1900 as 'something of a race riot' that followed a Black man's resistance to arrest. It is known only from a single sentence in a Mississippi weekly's state-news column, which gave no names, date, acts or casualties.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Newberry, South Carolina (1900)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at Newberry, South Carolina, in 1900 involved an unnamed fifteen-year-old Black boy who was jailed at Newberry on a charge of attempted assault on a white girl, Myrtle Farrow, and who, according to a brief press report, "narrowly escaped lynching." The episode is known only from a single sentence in a state-news column of the Anderson Intelligencer of 1 August 1900.

episodes.title: Pleasant View posse shooting
episodes.lead: The Pleasant View posse shooting was a gunfight on the night of August 7-8, 1900, near Pleasant View, Amherst County, Virginia, between a special constable's posse of eight white men and the Black family of Paul Smith, whom they came to arrest at home. All eight posse members were reported wounded, none fatally, and the Smiths surrendered on the understanding that they would be protected from a mob and not lynched. Virginia papers followed the case to forty-one indictments, while the Richmond Planet praised the family's armed defense of their home against a "mob."

episodes.title: Killing of Charley Tolbert
episodes.lead: The killing of Charley Tolbert took place on a county road near Rosanky, Texas, on the afternoon of August 16, 1900, when two white men on horseback beat and shot dead Tolbert, a Black man driving a wagon with his wife and child. According to the accounts, the attack followed Tolbert's refusal to give the road to the riders, and the attackers were never identified. Texas papers called it murder 'without provocation,' and the report reached the governor's Executive Office at Austin, where trouble among local Black residents was feared.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Fields
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam Fields was the killing of a young Black man by a mob of white men in Livingston Parish, Louisiana, in August 1900. Fields was accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Poche, and was shot to death, either after a posse chased him into the swamps or after a mob took him from officers. The killing reached papers across the country through New Orleans wire dispatches, but no coverage was found in the Black press.

episodes.title: Expulsion of a Black clergyman from Scranton, Kansas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of a Black clergyman from Scranton, Kansas, took place one evening in the summer of 1900, when several miners forced an elderly Black minister back onto the train he had just left at the Osage County town. The Topeka State Ledger reported the incident as proof that no Black man was allowed to stop in Scranton, and it called the town a second Gomorrah.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas J. Amos
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas J. Amos was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Cheneyville, Louisiana, before daylight on August 29, 1900, hours after the shotgun killing of Alanson G. Jackson, a white storekeeper. Accused of the killing, Amos was seized, was said to have confessed, and was hanged from a tree near the store where Jackson died. Papers across the country featured his reported offer to climb the tree, jump, and "show you how a man can die."

episodes.title: Monaghan mills shooting
episodes.lead: The Monaghan mills shooting was the pursuit and shooting of Bill Thompson, a Black laborer, by a group of white men at the Monaghan cotton mill construction site outside Greenville, South Carolina, on the morning of 14 August 1900. Thompson was shot in the jaw but survived, and nearly all the Black laborers on the job quit work. White papers reported it as a 'race riot', while a Black correspondent described a strike provoked by the white foreman.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tone Wiggins
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tone Wiggins took place in the Mt. Pleasant section of Nash County, North Carolina, in late August 1900, after Wiggins, a Black man, was arrested on suspicion of shooting a white farmer, Manoah M. Bissett. A dispatch reprinted in three white newspapers reported "threats of lynching the negro" while he was being tried, but described no move against him and gave no outcome.

episodes.title: Shooting at Will Nevels by a constable's deputy, Raleigh, 1900
episodes.lead: The shooting at Will Nevels was an incident on the night of Thursday, 23 August 1900, in which Jim Bryan, a deputy of Constable Ed. Potter, fired a pistol at Nevels, a Black man, near the gas house in the Fourth ward of Raleigh, North Carolina. The shot missed, and the mayor issued a warrant for the deputy's arrest, which led the Raleigh News & Observer to report the case under the headline "Arrested a Deputy."

episodes.title: Expulsion of Walter Bryant from Reading, Ohio
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Walter Bryant from Reading, Ohio, took place on the night of August 23, 1900, when a crowd of about forty seized Bryant, a Black youth, put a noose around his neck, tied him to a tree and drove him out of town. Bryant was released at the town limits with a warning that he would be lynched if he came back. The story, credited to the New York World, was reprinted in North Carolina under a headline stressing that the violence took place in Ohio.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Washington, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching in Washington, Louisiana, was a crowd's threat to lynch an unnamed Black man on the night of Saturday, August 18, 1900, after he allegedly fired at a constable trying to arrest him. Sheriff Swords took him to the Opelousas jail, and two local white papers disagreed over how near the crowd came to lynching him.

episodes.title: Russellville depot platform fight
episodes.lead: The Russellville depot platform fight was a clash in Russellville, Arkansas, in August 1900, in which a group of white boys drove some Black people off the railroad depot platform and followed them, and the Black men turned on them with knives. Will Davenport was fatally injured and Clarence Montgomery, a white man, was badly cut. The episode is known only from one short paragraph that circulated through Arkansas weeklies in the last week of August.

episodes.title: Shooting of Will Jones
episodes.lead: The shooting of Will Jones took place on the evening of August 26, 1900, in Newton, Kansas, when the city marshal shot a Black man by that name in the leg as he ran from an accusation of theft. Jones survived, and the papers, relying on the officer's side, said he admitted stealing a watch. The case ran as a short wire item and as a one-line entry in a column of Kansas news.

episodes.title: Hyndman circus beating of Black railroad workers
episodes.lead: The Hyndman circus beating of Black railroad workers took place on the night of August 20, 1900, at Hyndman, Pennsylvania, when William Baldwin, a white former foreman newly made a special policeman, clubbed, kicked and stoned Black laborers while trying to make an arrest. White newspapers reported it as a riot by the workers, under headlines such as "Riotous Negroes."

episodes.title: Mobbing of William Batmun
episodes.lead: The mobbing of William Batmun was an assault by a crowd on a Black man from Brooklyn at Coney Island, New York, in August 1900, after he escaped from an arresting officer. Police dispersed the crowd after it struck and kicked him, and he was fined $10 in police court. The episode is known from a single brief New York dispatch printed in a Wilmington, Delaware paper.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Black
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Black was a reported danger in 1900 that a Black man condemned to hang at Belair (Bel Air), Harford County, Maryland, for criminal assault on a fifteen-year-old girl would be seized and lynched before his execution. At the county's request Governor Smith sent a militia company to guard the hanging, and the sheriff brought Black from Baltimore after midnight and hanged him at 7:41 a.m. on August 31, before most of the town was awake. Wire reports presented the early hanging as a lynching averted, under headlines such as "Foils Mob and Hangs His Man."

episodes.title: Winchester circus riot
episodes.lead: The Winchester circus riot was a street fight between groups of white and Black men in Winchester, Virginia, on the morning of August 29, 1900, while a circus was being unloaded. A white man, William Custy, was knocked unconscious by a Black man named William Pratt, and whites then pursued the fleeing Black men, several of whom were reported severely beaten. Virginia papers called it a "race riot" and "a small race war"; Pratt was later reported arrested.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Fiqua
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Fiqua took place in downtown Chicago on the night of August 16, 1900, when a crowd chased a Black man accused of snatching a woman's pocketbook and tried to hang him. Police kept hold of him and brought him to the central station beaten but alive. Coming days after anti-Black riots in New Orleans and New York, the incident was reported nationally as a sign that the violence was spreading north.

episodes.title: Shooting at William Ford in Martinsburg
episodes.lead: The shooting at William Ford took place in Martinsburg, West Virginia, on the evening of Monday, August 20, 1900, when Policeman Dutrow fired at Ford, a Black transfer-wagon driver, as he fled arrest on a warrant. The shot missed, and Ford was caught after a street chase in which a crowd joined and stones were reportedly thrown at him. The local paper wrote that a "general race riot" had been feared.

episodes.title: Madison Square mob attack on William Jackson
episodes.lead: The Madison Square mob attack on William Jackson took place on the night of August 9, 1900, when a crowd at a band concert in Madison Square Park, New York City, surrounded a Black man just arrested by police and cried "Lynch him!" Police held off the crowd with nightsticks and took Jackson to the station, where he was charged with disorderly conduct. The story ran outside New York as a threatened lynching, headed "Negro Threatened With Lynching" in the Richmond Times.
